analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and its companion reconciliation law in full.
analysis.headline: The full repeal bill from Rep. Steve King drew 17 cosponsors, all Republicans, and never got a hearing or vote in the Democratic-run House before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill wipes out the Affordable Care Act (ObamaCare) and the companion law that amended it, retroactive to their 2010 enactment, and restores the old rules of health insurance, Medicare financing, and student loans as if those laws had never passed. That would end the ACA's subsidies that help people buy coverage, the Medicaid expansion, protections for pre-existing conditions, the requirement that insurers cover essential benefits, and taxes that fall mostly on higher earners and the health industry. It would also undo student-loan changes in the same law.
analysis.who_benefits: Higher-income households, health insurers, and drug makers. Repealing the ACA eliminates its Medicare and investment-income surtaxes, the annual fee on brand-name drug makers, and insurance regulations; it also ends the ACA's medical-liability limits that courts had applied against the drug industry's pricing (the rebates in the donut-hole fix). Workers with large employer health benefits and people who prefer skimpier, cheaper plans also gain.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals both the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act and the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010, effective as of each law's enactment, and restores or revives the provisions those laws amended [S3].

Restoring the pre-ACA rules would eliminate the ACA's taxes on investment income and high Medicare payrolls and the fees the ACA placed on brand-name drug makers and health insurers, benefits that go to higher earners and the health industry [S3].
It would also unwind the student-loan provisions in the same reconciliation law, returning federal student lending rules to the pre-2010 versions [S2].

analysis.who_pays: People who rely on the ACA. Roughly tens of millions gained coverage or affordability help under the ACA through Medicaid expansion, marketplace subsidies, and protections for pre-existing conditions; repeal removes all of it with no replacement in the bill. Seniors and people with disabilities would pay more for prescription drugs, since the donut-hole discount would be undone.
analysis.who_pays_short: People with pre-existing conditions and marketplace buyers

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no replacement provisions, so repeal would leave millions of previously uninsurable people facing medical underwriting or unaffordable premiums, and would eliminate premium help for middle-income buyers [S2].
Repeal is retroactive to 2010, which would unwind Medicaid expansion, the Medicare prescription-drug discounts, and student-loan changes that people have now relied on for a decade [S3].

An honest repeal case exists: ACA insurance rules pushed premiums up in some markets and the mandates added compliance costs for employers, and some Republicans argued repeal alone was cleaner than a partial replacement [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's gains fall on higher-income households and the health industry, while its costs fall on people who need coverage: those with pre-existing conditions, low-income adults in expansion states, and anyone using premium subsidies. The bill offers no offsetting protections, so its benefits and costs point in opposite directions, and the cost side is far larger for ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to eight House committees, then sent to subcommittees, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Steve King introduced the bill on January 3, 2019, the first day of the 116th Congress, with 17 Republican cosponsors [S1].
The House referred it to Energy and Commerce plus seven other committees, and later that month to three subcommittees, including the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee [S5].
The action history shows nothing after the subcommittee referrals; no committee took it up and the House never voted on it before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, brand-name drug makers, and higher-income taxpayers, who keep the ACA's taxes and rules off themselves because the repeal never advanced, while people with pre-existing conditions keep their protections.

for.name: Steve King
for.what_they_did: Introduced the full-repeal bill on the first day of the Congress.

against.name: Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: As Speaker, controlled the House floor schedule; no repeal bill reached a vote in the 116th Congress.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee on January 25, 2019, where it received no hearing or markup for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Republican (18 of 197 House Republicans), and the bill never moved in a House controlled by Democrats; no Democrat supported it in the record.

industries.note: Repeal would end ACA rules limiting what they can keep for administration and profit and their fee under the law, but also strip them of the mandate- and subsidy-driven customer base. Under repeal they regain the ability to deny or surcharge people with pre-existing conditions, which is why their interest runs against the public's here.
The ACA imposed an annual fee on brand-name drug makers and required the 50 percent donut-hole discount; repeal removes both, costing seniors and the government more for drugs.
Repeal eliminates the ACA's investment-income surtax and Medicare payroll surtax on top earners, which are the largest direct tax losses from repeal.
